claim: Go breaks the input into tokens by taking the longest sequence of characters that forms a valid token as the next token.
quote: While breaking the input into tokens, the next token is the longest sequence of characters that form a valid token.

claim: Go automatically inserts a semicolon into the token stream immediately after a line's final token when that token is an identifier, an integer, floating-point, imaginary, rune, or string literal, one of the keywords break, continue, fallthrough or return, or one of the operators and punctuation ++, --, ), ] or }.
quote:
When the input is broken into tokens, a semicolon is automatically inserted into the token stream immediately after a line's final token if that token is
- an identifier
- an integer, floating-point, imaginary, rune, or string literal
- one of the keywords break, continue, fallthrough, or return
- one of the operators and punctuation ++, --, ), ], or }

claim: Go reserves 25 keywords, none of which may be used as identifiers.
quote:
The following keywords are reserved and may not be used as identifiers.

break        default      func         interface    select
case         defer        go           map          struct
chan         else         goto         package      switch
const        fallthrough  if           range        type
continue     for          import       return       var

claim: Once the input stream has been parsed into preprocessing tokens up to a given character, the next preprocessing token is the longest sequence of characters that could constitute a preprocessing token.
quote: If the input stream has been parsed into preprocessing tokens up to a given character, the next preprocessing token is the longest sequence of characters that could constitute a preprocessing token.

claim: C parses the fragment x+++++y as x ++ ++ + y, which violates a constraint on increment operators, even though the parse x ++ + ++ y might yield a correct expression.
quote: The program fragment x+++++y is parsed as x ++ ++ + y, which violates a constraint on increment operators, even though the parse x ++ + ++ y might yield a correct expression.

claim: The scanner reads a stream of characters and produces a stream of words, aggregating characters into words, applying rules to decide whether each word is legal in the source language, and assigning a valid word a syntactic category.
quote: The scanner, or lexical analyzer, reads a stream of characters and produces a stream of words. It aggregates characters to form words and applies a set of rules to determine whether or not each word is legal in the source language. If the word is valid, the scanner assigns it a syntactic category, or part of speech.

claim: Although efficient parsing techniques weakened the original efficiency argument for separating scanning from parsing, scanners are still built separately because it provides a clean separation of concerns between lexical structure and syntactic structure.
quote: The advent of efficient parsing techniques weakened this argument, but the practice of building scanners persists because it provides a clean separation of concerns between lexical structure and syntactic structure.

claim: Thompson's 1968 compiler accepted a regular expression as its source language and produced an IBM 7094 program as its object language.
quote: The compiler accepts a regular expression as source language and produces an IBM 7094 program as object language.

claim: Thompson's regular expression implementation was for his QED editor running on CTSS.
quote: Thompson's regular expression implementation was for his QED editor running on the CTSS

claim: Thompson's construction creates exactly one NFA state per character or metacharacter in the regex, excluding parentheses, so the number of NFA states is at most the length of the regex.
quote: this technique creates exactly one state per character or metacharacter in the regular expression, excluding parentheses. Therefore the number of states in the final NFA is at most equal to the length of the original regular expression.

claim: For a regular expression of length m run on text of length n, the Thompson NFA simulation requires O(mn) time.
quote: For a regular expression of length m run on text of length n, the Thompson NFA requires O(mn) time.

claim: On the regex a?^n a^n matched against a^n (n = 29), Perl requires over sixty seconds while the Thompson NFA requires twenty microseconds.
quote: Notice that Perl requires over sixty seconds to match a 29-character string. The other approach, labeled Thompson NFA for reasons that will be explained later, requires twenty microseconds to match the string.

claim: Perl, PCRE, Python and Ruby use recursive backtracking, and PCRE stops getting the right answer at n=23 because it aborts the recursion after a maximum number of steps.
quote: From the graph it is clear that Perl, PCRE, Python, and Ruby are all using recursive backtracking. PCRE stops getting the right answer at n=23, because it aborts the recursive backtracking after a maximum number of steps.

claim: Michael Rabin and Dana Scott introduced non-deterministic finite automata and the concept of non-determinism in 1959.
quote: Michael Rabin and Dana Scott introduced non-deterministic finite automata and the concept of non-determinism in 1959

claim: In a 1956 paper, Kleene introduced the notion of regular expression and proved that regular-expression languages and finite-automata languages are the same class (Kleene's Theorem).
quote: In a 1956 paper, Kleene introduced the notion of regular expression, and proved that the languages specified by regular expressions and the languages generated by finite automata constituted the same class, a basic result today known as Kleene's Theorem.

claim: Go's regexp package is guaranteed to run in time linear in the size of the input.
quote: The regexp implementation provided by this package is guaranteed to run in time linear in the size of the input.

claim: In Engineering a Compiler's subset construction, the main loop repeatedly removes one configuration q from a worklist and uses the function Delta to compute its transitions.
quote: The while loop repeatedly removes a configuration q from the worklist and uses Delta to compute its potential transitions.

claim: The epsilon-closure of a set of NFA states S is the set of states reachable from S by epsilon transitions, including S itself.
quote: For any S⊆Q, define the ϵ-closure of S to be the set of states reachable from S by ϵ transitions (incl. S)

locator: section 2.4.1 'Equivalence of NFAs and DFAs', p. 45
claim: Engineering a Compiler says the subset construction needs one DFA state for each configuration (set of active states) of the NFA, so the resulting DFA may have exponentially more states than the NFA.
quote: To simulate the behavior of the nfa, we need a dfa with a state for each configuration of the nfa. As a result, the dfa may have exponentially more states than the nfa.

claim: An NFA with n+1 states can require no fewer than 2^n DFA states; the witnessing language is the strings whose n-th symbol from the end is 1.
quote: There is an NFA N with n + 1 states that has no equivalent DFA with fewer than 2n states. L(N) = {x1c2 c3 · · · cn : x ∈ {0, 1}∗ , ci ∈ {0, 1}}.

claim: Hopcroft's minimization algorithm's asymptotic running time in a worst-case analysis is bounded by k n log n, where k is a constant and n is the number of states.
quote: The asymptotic running time of the algorithm is bounded by knlogn where k is some constant and n is the number of states.

locator: section 2.6.2 'Another Approach to DFA Minimization: Brzozowski's Algorithm', p. 75
claim: Engineering a Compiler presents Brzozowski's algorithm as an alternative DFA minimization that directly constructs the minimal DFA from an NFA.
quote: Brzozowski used this observation to devise an alternative dfa minimization algorithm that directly constructs the minimal dfa from an nfa.

claim: For every regular language there is a unique minimal-state DFA, unique up to relabeling of the states.
quote: For every regular language A, there is a unique (up to re-labeling of the states) minimal-state DFA M* such that A = L(M*).

locator: section 2.4.5 'Using a DFA as a Recognizer', p. 58
claim: If the DFA overshoots and reaches a non-accepting state, the recognizer backs up to the most recent accepting state, which yields the longest valid prefix.
quote: If the dfa passed through one or more accepting states on its way to s, the recognizer should back up to the most recent such state. This strategy matches the longest valid prefix in the input string.

locator: section 2.4.5 'Using a DFA as a Recognizer', p. 58
claim: When an accepting DFA state matches several patterns (token kinds), scanner generators return the syntactic category of the highest-priority pattern.
quote: Most scanner-generator tools allow the compiler writer to specify a priority among patterns. When the recognizer matches multiple patterns, it returns the syntactic category of the highest-priority pattern.

claim: The Go compiler's lexer is a scanner implemented in one file that advances one token per call to next.
quote: This file implements scanner, a lexical tokenizer for Go source. After initialization, consecutive calls of next advance the scanner one token at a time.

claim: After scanning a whole identifier into lit, the compiler scanner decides whether it is a keyword by hashing lit and looking it up in keywordMap, doing so only for identifiers of length two or more.
go/scanner's Scan returns three values: the token position, the token, and its literal string when applicable.
quote: Scan scans the next token and returns the token position, the token, and its literal string if applicable. The source end is indicated by token.EOF.

claim: For an inserted semicolon, go/scanner reports the SEMICOLON token with the literal string "\n"; a semicolon actually present in the source gets the literal ";".
quote: If the returned token is token.SEMICOLON, the corresponding literal string is ";" if the semicolon was present in the source, and "\n" if the semicolon was inserted because of a newline or at EOF.

locator: section 7, How the Input Is Matched
claim: flex takes the match covering the most text, and when two or more matches are of the same length it chooses the rule listed first in the input file.
quote: If it finds more than one match, it takes the one matching the most text (for trailing context rules, this includes the length of the trailing part, even though it will then be returned to the input). If it finds two or more matches of the same length, the rule listed first in the flex input file is chosen.

claim: flex warns "rule cannot be matched" for a rule that can never match because it follows other rules that will always match the same text.
quote: 'warning, rule cannot be matched' indicates that the given rule cannot be matched because it follows other rules that will always match the same text as it.

claim: re2c compiles regular expressions to deterministic finite automata and translates them into directly coded (not table-driven) lexers in the target language.
quote: The primary focus of re2c is on generating fast code: it compiles regular expressions to deterministic finite automata and translates them into direct-coded lexers in the target language (such lexers are generally faster and easier to debug than their table-driven analogues).

claim: re2c's own site names php, ninja, yasm, spamassassin, BRL-CAD and wake among the open-source projects that use it.
quote: re2c is used in other open-source projects, such as php, ninja, yasm, spamassassin, BRL-CAD, wake, etc.

quote: Although it is popular to implement lexers as generated finite state machines, the lexer in rustc_lexer is hand-written.

quote: The Lexer class provides the mechanics of lexing tokens out of a source buffer and deciding what they mean.

claim: By default flex generates a C source file defining yylex.
quote: flex generates as output a C source file, lex.yy.c by default, which defines a routine yylex().

quote: In both cases, whether a diagnostic is needed or not is dependent upon the lexer’s state.

quote: Each token has its line and col variables set to the line and column of the first character of the token.

claim: Regular-expression alternation matches either operand language, and concatenation matches strings from one followed by strings from the other.
quote: Two regular expressions can be alternated or concatenated to form a new regular expression: if e1 matches s and e2 matches t, then e1|e2 matches s or t, and e1e2 matches st.

claim: An NFA accepts when some path consumes the input and reaches a matching state; unlabeled edges consume no input.
quote: An NFA matches an input string if there is some way it can read the string and follow arrows to a matching state. Sometimes it is convenient to let NFAs have arrows with no corresponding input character.

claim: Backreferences add expressive power beyond theoretical regular expressions.
quote: One common regular expression extension that does provide additional power is called backreferences.

claim: C postfix increment and decrement require a modifiable lvalue of real or pointer type.
quote: The operand of the postfix increment or decrement operator shall have atomic, qualified, or unqualified real or pointer type, and shall be a modifiable lvalue.

claim: C postfix increment yields the operand value and increments the operand as a side effect.
quote: The result of the postfix ++ operator is the value of the operand. As a side effect, the value of the operand object is incremented (that is, the value 1 of the appropriate type is added to it).

claim: C postfix decrement is analogous to postfix increment but subtracts one from the operand.
quote: The postfix -- operator is analogous to the postfix ++ operator, except that the value of the operand is decremented (that is, the value 1 of the appropriate type is subtracted from it).
